title: CAP, PACELC and consistency models
subtitle: When the network splits, every copy of your data must choose between answering and being right. The rest of the time, it chooses between fast and right.

c.v: in two regions, Mumbai and Singapore. There are 500 pairs. The stock count lives in a database that copies data between the regions. Both regions accept orders.

Ten minutes into the sale, the link between the regions breaks for four minutes. Both sides keep selling. Each side thinks it has the full count. When the link comes back, the team finds 620 orders for 500 pairs. Support spends a week on refunds and apologies.
In the same company, the payments team uses a different database. During the same four minutes, it refused every write in Singapore. Those users saw "Payment failed, try again".

Both teams wrote the same thing in the incident channel: "the database broke". It did not. Each database did exactly what it was built to do. Nobody had written down which choice the business wanted. This story is made up, but each part of it happens in real systems.

During a partition, a replica that gets a request has only two options:
It may return old data, or accept a write that conflicts with the other side. The system stays available.
It does not answer until it can check with the other side. The data stays consistent.
. Gilbert and Lynch proved it in 2002. No system can promise both consistency and availability when messages between nodes can be lost.
People often say CAP means "pick 2 of 3". Eric Brewer presented the idea in a keynote talk in 2000.
In 2012 he wrote that "2 of 3" is misleading.
You cannot simply pick "no partitions", because networks can fail.
But partitions are rare. When there is no partition, a system can be both consistent and available.

CAP is a rule for one bad moment: the network is split. In that moment, each cut-off replica chooses between answering and being right. The rest of the time, the real choice is between fast and right.
Step through the shoe sale with one item left. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
What C and A mean in CAP
The words in CAP are narrow. Consistency means
: the system must act as if there is one copy and each operation happens at one instant.
It is not the C in
Availability means every request that reaches a working node gets an answer that is not an error. Not "most requests", and not "some node answers".
With these strict meanings, many real databases are neither CP nor AP. Kleppmann gives an example: one
. A client cut off from the leader cannot write, so it is not available. Reads from a lagging follower can be stale, so it is not linearizable either.
So do not label a whole database. Ask what each operation does during a partition.
PACELC: the trade you make every day
Abadi pointed out a second trade-off that matters more day to day.

Why is there a trade when the network is fine? As soon as you copy data, a consistent read or write must coordinate with other replicas or a leader. That takes time. Over long distances, you cannot avoid this wait.
Abadi gives an example from a study of Cassandra. Reads that check several replicas were compared with reads from any one replica. The
difference could be a factor of four or more.
Abadi classified well-known systems by their original default settings:
Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak. They give up consistency during a partition, and for lower latency in normal running.
VoltDB/H-Store, Megastore, BigTable and HBase. They pay in availability and latency to stay consistent.
Yahoo's PNUTS. Fast and less consistent normally, but it refuses updates to data whose master node is cut off by a partition.

Many of these systems let you change the trade. In Cassandra-style stores, you can ask more replicas to answer each read and write. You get more consistency, though still not linearizability, and pay with latency.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: "If the network splits right now, should this fail or should it accept and fix later?"
Treat "CP" and "AP" in vendor docs as a hint, not a fact. Read which operations wait, which refuse, and what the default settings are.
Measure the latency cost. A consistent read in another region costs a round trip on every request, partition or not.
If you choose AP, design the repair before launch: how to detect conflicts, which side wins, and who tells the customer. Brewer calls this partition recovery.
Use stronger models only where they are worth the cost. A stock count may need linearizable writes. The product description next to it does not.
Test with a real partition. Cut the network between replicas in a test environment, and watch what your app does.
"Here is our order service. List every database write. For each, tell me what happens if the replicas in two regions cannot talk for 5 minutes, with our current settings."
"We use Cassandra with replication factor 3. Explain which read and write consistency levels give us read-your-writes for one user, and what each choice costs in latency."
"Write a test that starts two replicas, cuts the network between them, writes on both sides, heals the network, and checks that our conflict rule keeps both orders."
The agent's claims about a database's behaviour match that database's own docs and version. CAP labels on blogs are often wrong.
The settings it suggests are the ones your code really sends. Many clients have their own default
The partition test cuts the network between replicas. Killing a node is a different failure.
The conflict rule never silently drops a paid order or a payment.
Every operation that needs linearizable behaviour is listed, and a person agreed to its latency cost.

q.v: According to CAP, when must a system choose between consistency and availability?

options.v: All the time. You can only ever have 2 of the 3 properties.
Only while there is a network partition between its nodes.

why.v: CAP is about the moment the network loses messages. With no partition, a system can be both consistent and available.

q.v: A replica is cut off from the others. It refuses a write and returns an error. What did it choose?

why.v: It stayed correct by refusing the write. In CAP, a node that is up but returns an error instead of doing the work is not available.

q.v: What does the "ELC" part of PACELC describe?

options.v: What the system does during a partition.
The trade between latency and consistency when there is no partition.
The trade between cost and latency.

why.v: Else (E), in normal running, the system trades latency (L) against consistency (C). Waiting for other replicas makes a read or write slower.

q.v: Ana posts a comment. Ben replies to it. Under causal consistency, what can Chen never see?

options.v: Both of them, a few seconds late.

why.v: The reply depends on the comment. Causal consistency shows related operations in the same order to everyone.

q.v: Your service uses one Postgres leader with async read replicas. Is it CP or AP in the strict CAP sense?

options.v: CP, because there is one leader.
Neither. Clients cut off from the leader cannot write, and replica reads can be stale.

why.v: Kleppmann uses this setup, one leader with async followers, to show why the CP/AP labels often do not fit real systems.

sources.title: Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch, “Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services”, ACM SIGACT News, 2002
sources.note: The proof of CAP. Section 2 defines consistency, availability and partition tolerance exactly. Theorem 1 is the result.

sources.title: Eric Brewer, “CAP Twelve Years Later: How the ‘Rules’ Have Changed”, IEEE Computer, 2012
sources.note: Brewer explains why "2 of 3" is misleading, and how to detect a partition, limit some operations, and recover after it.

sources.title: Daniel J. Abadi, “Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design”, IEEE Computer, February 2012
sources.note: The PACELC paper. Explains the latency versus consistency trade-off and classifies Dynamo, Cassandra, PNUTS, MongoDB and others.

sources.title: Martin Kleppmann, “Please stop calling databases CP or AP” (2015)
sources.note: Why most real databases are neither CP nor AP in CAP's strict sense, and what to say instead.

sources.title: Jepsen, Consistency models: Linearizability
sources.note: A short, exact definition, and why it cannot stay available during a partition.

sources.title: Jepsen, Consistency models: Sequential consistency
sources.note: Like linearizability, but without the real-time rule.

sources.title: Jepsen, Consistency models: Causal consistency
sources.note: Related operations appear in the same order everywhere. Available during a partition if clients stay on one server.

sources.title: Jepsen, Consistency models: Read Your Writes
sources.note: A short, exact definition of the read-your-writes guarantee.

sources.title: Werner Vogels, “Eventually Consistent – Revisited” (2008)
sources.note: Defines eventual consistency, read-your-writes and other client-side guarantees.
